If anyone wants to talk philosophy, this is something I've been dying to discuss: a common argument against God is that there is no evidence that he exists, so occam's razor supports the belief that there is no God.

My response is that this is only when the two competing theories have equal explanatory power. For example, there is a theory that everything is made of water. This competes with the periodic table of elements. The reason we go with the latter is that it has greater explanatory power even though the former proposes less entities.

So, my question is where does matter come from. For the belief in God, I propose one entity. He explains everything as he created everything. If there is no God, then you say the big bang. Then where did that come from. And to whatever created that, where did that come from. This goes on and on and one must propose more and more entities. My argument is then that 1) it is not as simple as it requires more proposed entities and 2) it never gets to the same explanatory power as just a belief in God. And so, a belief in God is actually favorable philosophically.

I'm not sure how [1] points to the belief in God being more favorable. To choose simplicity over a multi-variable scenario for the sake of simplicity would be more useful if one's goal were to possess an easily understandable compendium of knowledge that hinges upon a single unprovable assumption, but from a vantage point of seeking to understand the universe for what it is and constructing that knowledge axiomatically, a philosophical train of thought dependent upon God would appear counterproductive and never provably applicable due to its unfalsifiable/unprovable basis. To me, that appears to be an "easy way out" sort of justification rather than one that demonstrates the objective favorability of that assumption.

As for [2]... we, as parts of the universe seeking to understand itself, can't know that until we reach the end of intelligent species. A belief in God allows you the opportunity to devise your own meaning of the universe in your lifetime only because an omniscient, omnipresent being is, by definition, an entity that encompasses everything and thus your philosophy of everything need only rest upon the entity that you have created. The "God" entity is an all-encompassing explanatory power because it is constructed as one.

I don't frequently delve into that kind of thought, so please do point out if I've committed any fallacies in my reasoning or misinterpreted what you said :3 I see God as a "top-down" way of analyzing the universe (starting at the conclusion and breaking it apart into the smallest bits of knowledge) and axiomatic reasoning as a "bottom-up" approach (taking the smallest pieces of irrefutable truths and building upon those, the entire picture being your conclusion). The former causes so much doubt that, for me, is impossible to cast aside, and so I choose the latter.

My argument was more to disprove the argument against God that I've heard many say. I don't think there is a proof that God exists or one that he doesn't exist. I think either belief that He exists or does not takes faith.

I'm having some trouble with the first paragraph. I think the way I view God may be different than yours, so I'm not sure which is the clause that relates to God and which isn't.

You say, "but from a vantage point of seeking to understand the universe for what it is and constructing that knowledge axiomatically." That is what I'm trying to do and God is an important axiom in my theory. You see the universe as a continuum (correct me if I'm wrong) and we only know as far back as the big bang and we are slowly learning more and more. You may not recognized it, but it seems that a belief that there is no god is an important axiom in your theory; that's the only way for the continuum to not have a beginning. I believe that at one point God created matter; that may have been at the big bang, or that may have been whatever fed into the big bang. From my perspective a philosophical train of thought that is dependent upon the belief that there is no God is equally counterproductive and never provably applicable due to its unfalsifiable/unprovable basis. Thus, the only way to choose between my theory and yours is gut instinct, or as we call it: faith.

Talking about the big bang and Islam, here is an interesting passages from the quran that relates to it. This one is targeted to people that do not believe in God: "Have those who disbelieved not considered that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them and made from water every living thing? Then will they not believe?" http://quran.com/21/30 The verb "separated" is also often translated as "ripped apart." I like it because I take it as saying that the big bang should be taken as evidence of the existence of God.

To your second paragraph, I say the same thing back. I agree we are parts of the universe trying to understand itself and we can't know that God exists for certain until we reach the end of intelligent species. I can see why the second part of the paragraph would be enticing to think, but, again, I do not think there is a proof that God doesn't exist.

It's been a fun discussion so far!

You see the universe as a continuum (correct me if I'm wrong)

In the sense that time is a dimension within which our reality exists, then maybe. It has not been demonstrated to be either cyclical or non-cyclical (a "closed" dimension), because we have not seen beyond the Big Bang yet*. Even supposing that time was without end 'going backward or forward', what is the reasoning that this would necessitate that God does or does not exist? That seems like a random assertion.

You may not recognized it, but it seems that a belief that there is no god is an important axiom in your theory; that's the only way for the continuum to not have a beginning.

I didn't assume either that God is nonexistent or that the supposed continuum is without beginning or end (our collection of knowledge does not yet allow us to reject or affirm the finiteness of time). Both God and his nonexistence are non-axioms, as they are not universally self-evident truths that are irrefutable without utilizing them as premises; an unfalsifiable statement can never be an axiom because the positive and negative are equally unprovable and refute each other without requiring affirmation of the other (it would be a paradox otherwise). Nothing in my reasoning is dependent upon the antithesis of your positive assumption that there is a God, as I do not depend upon any validity of the concept. God as a concept is unfalsifiable and useless as either a negative or a positive in axiomatic reasoning.

As for the Big Bang being 'evidence' that God exists... I just don't see how. That argument sounds just like Aquinas' "First Clause" 'proof', which just asserts God as the cause of an unexplained effect. There's also no reason that this supposed God would not himself need a reason to exist, and his reason to exist need a reason to exist, ad infinitum.

My second paragraph (and the rest of my comment) was not intended as reasoning that God does not exist (I don't know how I could hope to prove that after several thousands of years of religious scholars have attempted it). There is just no convincing reasoning as to why assuming that he does is favorable to the bottom-up model, which does not utilize assumptions. An inherent property of reason is that it is devoid of faith — I do not have "faith" in reason as one would a God.

It does indeed require faith to definitively assert either position on God's existence (because S/He is an unfalsifiable entity), but I never claimed either the positive or the negative. There is simply no evidence or undeniably true chain of logic supporting either claim, which is why I do not claim/support affirmation or denial.
